questions.topic: Definition of type II glass containers
questions.question: According to Ph. Eur. 3.2.1, how are Type II glass containers defined?

options.A: Neutral borosilicate glass whose high hydrolytic resistance comes from the chemical composition of the glass network itself, not from any surface treatment
options.B: Usually soda-lime-silica glass with only moderate hydrolytic resistance, mostly used for non-parenteral preparations
options.C: Usually soda-lime-silica glass whose high hydrolytic resistance is due to suitable treatment of the inner surface
options.D: Usually borosilicate glass whose high hydrolytic resistance is due to a coating applied to the outer surface, not the inner surface

questions.explanation: Type II is usually soda-lime-silica glass that obtains its high hydrolytic resistance from treatment of the inner surface. Type I owes it to the composition of the glass itself (neutral glass), and Type III has only moderate hydrolytic resistance.

questions.question: Someone proposes Type III glass containers for a freeze-dried injectable powder. According to the general recommendations of Ph. Eur. 3.2.1, how should this be judged?

options.A: Not suitable, because the general recommendation for Type III with powders for injection excludes freeze-dried products, and a container with higher hydrolytic resistance should be used
options.B: Acceptable, because Type III is generally suitable for all powders for injection, including freeze-dried products
options.C: Acceptable, because Type III is suitable for all aqueous injectable preparations, and freeze-dried products only need additional evaluation
options.D: Not suitable, because Type III is only for non-parenteral preparations and must not be used for any powder or liquid for injection

questions.explanation: Type III is generally suitable for non-aqueous injectable preparations, powders for injection (except freeze-dried products), and non-parenteral preparations; containers with higher hydrolytic resistance than the recommended type can generally also be used. The manufacturer remains responsible for confirming the suitability of the container.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about glass delamination in Ph. Eur. 3.2.1 is correct?

options.A: If no flakes are seen within one month of filling the container, it can be concluded that delamination will not occur later
options.B: Delamination depends only on the temperature-time profile of the manufacturing process and not on the composition of the preparation, buffer type, or ionic strength
options.C: A short-term accelerated test with the preparation in contact with the glass is enough to fully replace stability testing under normal conditions of use
options.D: Flakes may appear only several months after filling, and both buffers and ionic strength are risk factors

questions.explanation: The interaction between glass and the preparation needs incubation time, and flakes may appear only several months after filling; the composition of the preparation, citrate or phosphate buffers, ionic strength, and process conditions are all risk factors. Accelerated tests are only a predictive tool, and full compatibility must still be confirmed by stability testing under normal conditions.

questions.topic: Choosing a test for glass type (Table 3.2.1.-1)
questions.question: According to Table 3.2.1.-1, which test should be used to distinguish Type I glass containers from Type II and Type III?

options.A: Test A (surface test), because it can distinguish Type I from Type II and also Type III
options.B: Test B (glass grains test) or Test C (etching test); Test A can only distinguish Type I/II from Type III
options.C: Only Test B, because Test C is used only to identify Type III containers and cannot distinguish Type I
options.D: Test A plus the arsenic test, both of which are required to determine the type of a Type I glass container

questions.explanation: Test A is used to distinguish Type I and II from Type III; to distinguish Type I from Type II and III, Test B or Test C must be used. If high hydrolytic resistance may be due to composition or to surface treatment, Tests A and B, or Tests A and C, are used together.

questions.question: Six vials from a batch have a mean brimful capacity of 12.0 mL. According to Ph. Eur. 3.2.1, what should the filling volume of this batch of vials be when performing the test?

options.A: 12.0 mL, the mean brimful capacity itself; the filling volume equals the brimful capacity
options.B: 10.0 mL, using the nominal capacity as the filling volume rather than the measured mean
options.C: 10.8 mL, the mean brimful capacity multiplied by 0.9 and expressed to 1 decimal place
options.D: 9.6 mL, the mean brimful capacity multiplied by 0.8 and expressed to 1 decimal place

questions.explanation: For vials and bottles, the filling volume is 90% of the brimful capacity: 12.0 × 0.9 = 10.8 mL. Ampoules are instead filled to the height of the shoulder rather than calculated as 90%.

questions.question: In the reference thermal cycle of Test A, once the temperature inside the container reaches 121 °C, what are the holding time and the subsequent cooling requirement?

options.A: Hold at 121 ± 1 °C for 60 ± 1 min, then cool to 100 °C within 40-44 min
options.B: Hold at 121 ± 1 °C for 30 ± 1 min, then cool to 100 °C within 40-44 min
options.C: Hold at 121 ± 1 °C for 60 ± 1 min, then cool to 100 °C within 20-22 min
options.D: Hold at 121 ± 1 °C for 10 ± 1 min, then cool to room temperature within 20-30 min

questions.explanation: Test A holds at 121 ± 1 °C for 60 ± 1 min, then cools to 100 °C within 40-44 min. The 30 ± 1 min hold is for Test B (glass grains), so do not confuse them; the 10 ± 1 min is the intermediate hold at 100 °C.

questions.question: Why must the autoclave for Test A be calibrated, before first use, with a calibrated thermocouple or resistance thermometer placed inside a container?

options.A: Because the thermometer on the chamber cannot measure above 100 °C, so an external probe must be used
options.B: Because a thermocouple must confirm every routine run before the test result can be judged valid and released
options.C: Because the HCl concentration used for titration must be adjusted for each container volume, so the temperature inside the container must be measured first
options.D: Because the actual temperatures in the chamber and inside the container can differ significantly, and it must be confirmed that 121 ± 1 °C is reached inside the container

questions.explanation: The purpose of calibration is to confirm that the autoclave settings bring the temperature inside the containers to 121 ± 1 °C, because the temperature in the chamber and inside the container can differ significantly. Once calibration is valid, routine runs no longer need a thermocouple, but the calibration must be periodically confirmed as still valid.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the titration step and the expression of results in Test A?

options.A: Titrate with 0.02 M HCl within 4 h of removal from the autoclave; express the result as mL of HCl consumed per gram of glass
options.B: Titrate with 0.01 M HCl within 1 h of removal, subtract the blank, and express the result as mL of HCl consumed per 100 mL
options.C: Titrate with 0.01 M HCl the day after cooling, without a blank, and express the result as µg of sodium oxide per gram of glass
options.D: Titrate with 0.02 M NaOH within 1 h of removal, subtract the blank, and express the result as mL of NaOH consumed per 100 mL

questions.explanation: In Test A, titration with 0.01 M HCl and methyl red must be done within 1 h after the containers leave the autoclave, the blank is subtracted, and the result is mL of 0.01 M HCl per 100 mL. Titration with 0.02 M HCl, expressed per gram, belongs to Test B.

questions.question: A batch of Type I containers has a filling volume of 15 mL and a Test A result of 0.90 mL (0.01 M HCl per 100 mL). According to Table 3.2.1.-3, how is this result judged?

options.A: Fails, because the limit for Type I/II in this volume range is 0.80 mL, and 0.90 mL exceeds it
options.B: Passes, because the limit for Type I/II in this volume range is 1.0 mL, and 0.90 mL is below that limit
options.C: Passes, because the limit for this volume range is 8.1 mL, and 0.90 mL is far below that limit, so there is no concern
options.D: Fails, because the limit for Type I/II in this volume range is 0.50 mL, and 0.90 mL exceeds it

questions.explanation: For filling volumes from 10 mL up to 20 mL, the limit is 0.80 mL for Types I/II and 8.1 mL for Type III; 0.90 mL exceeds the Type I limit. 1.0 mL is the limit for the 5-10 mL range, and 8.1 mL is the Type III limit.

questions.question: What are the limits of Test B (glass grains test) for each type of glass container?

options.A: Type I: not more than 0.85 mL of 0.02 M HCl per gram of glass; Types II and III: not more than 0.1 mL
options.B: Type I: not more than 0.1 mL of 0.01 M HCl per gram of glass; Types II and III: not more than 0.85 mL
options.C: Type I: not more than 0.1 mL of 0.02 M HCl per gram of glass; Types II and III: not more than 0.85 mL
options.D: Types I and II: not more than 0.1 mL of 0.02 M HCl per gram of glass; Type III: not more than 0.85 mL

questions.explanation: Test B uses 0.02 M HCl; Type I is not more than 0.1 mL/g, and Types II and III are not more than 0.85 mL/g. This is also why Test B can distinguish Type I from Types II and III; if Type II had the same limit as Type I, they could not be distinguished.

questions.question: A vial is etched in Test C (HF and HCl mixed 1:9 by volume, left to stand for 10 min), and the value then measured by the Test A procedure is about 7 times that of the original surface. How should this be interpreted?

options.A: The container has no surface treatment, because the value after etching should be much higher than the original surface
options.B: The test is invalid, because the result after etching must be within 2 times the value of the original surface
options.C: Etching has destroyed the bulk of the glass, so the classification should be redone with Test B and the Test C result disregarded
options.D: The inner surface of the container has been treated, and its high hydrolytic resistance comes from the treatment rather than from the glass composition itself

questions.explanation: If the result after etching is markedly higher than that of the original surface (about 5 to 10 times), the sample has been surface treated. If it has not been surface treated, the value after etching is similar to the original value (slightly lower for ampoules).

questions.question: Comparing the Test C and Test A results, according to Table 3.2.1.-4, how do Type I and Type II containers differ?

options.A: For Type I, the Test C value is much higher than the Test A value; for Type II, the two values are similar, with no clear gap
options.B: For Type I, the two are similar; for Type II, the Test C value greatly exceeds Test A and is similar to Type III
options.C: For both types, the Test C value is much higher than the Test A value, and the difference is that the Type II value exceeds that of Type III
options.D: For both types, the Test C value is similar to the Test A value, and Test B must be used instead to distinguish the two types

questions.explanation: The high hydrolytic resistance of Type I comes from the composition itself, so the value hardly changes after the surface is etched away; Type II depends on surface treatment, so after etching removes the treated layer the value rises sharply to a level similar to, but not greater than, Type III.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct regarding the arsenic test in Ph. Eur. 3.2.1?

options.A: All glass containers must be tested, using the extract after Test C etching, with a limit of not more than 0.1 ppm As
options.B: Only coloured glass containers must be tested, using the extract from Test B, with a limit of not more than 0.1 ppm As
options.C: It applies to containers for aqueous parenteral preparations, using the extract of Type I and II containers from Test A, with a limit of 0.1 ppm
options.D: It applies to containers for aqueous parenteral preparations, using the extract of Type I and II containers from Test A, with a limit of not more than 1 ppm As

questions.explanation: The arsenic test applies to glass containers for aqueous parenteral preparations, using the extract obtained from Type I and II containers autoclaved according to Test A (121 °C, 1 h), determined by hydride generation AAS, with a limit of not more than 0.1 ppm As.

questions.topic: Spectral transmission limit for non-parenteral coloured glass
questions.question: What is the limit for spectral transmission of coloured glass containers used for non-parenteral preparations?

options.A: Not more than 10% at any wavelength between 290 and 450 nm, regardless of container type and capacity
options.B: Mean value not more than 10% between 290 and 450 nm, and graded by nominal capacity
options.C: Not more than 10% at any wavelength between 290 and 450 nm, but applicable only to containers of 1 mL or less
options.D: Not more than 10% at any wavelength between 400 and 800 nm, regardless of container type and capacity

questions.explanation: For coloured containers for non-parenteral preparations, transmission at any wavelength between 290 and 450 nm must not exceed 10%, irrespective of type and capacity. For coloured containers for parenteral preparations, limits are set by nominal capacity and closure method according to Table 3.2.1.-5.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about determining surface hydrolytic resistance by flame spectrometry in the Annex is correct?

options.A: Its results are equivalent to the titration method, and the two methods can be used interchangeably without further justification or authorisation
options.B: It is the pharmacopoeial reference method, and the titration method may be used for small containers only in exceptional, authorised cases
options.C: It needs a larger volume of extract than the titration method, so it suits only large-capacity containers and cannot analyse small ones
options.D: It needs less extract and can be used on small containers to assess within-batch homogeneity, but it is not equivalent to titration and may be used only with authorisation

questions.explanation: The spectrometric method needs less extract, can be used on small individual containers, and can assess within-batch homogeneity; however, its results are not equivalent to or interchangeable with titration. Titration is the pharmacopoeial reference method, and the spectrometric method is used only where justified and authorised.
